column1: Why is UART considered 'asynchronous' compared to SPI or I²C?
column2: UART transmits no dedicated clock signal; both transmitter and receiver must be independently preconfigured to the same baud rate (prior agreement) rather than embedding clock timing in a signal line.

column1: What is the structure of a standard UART frame?
column2: 1 start bit (logic low) → 5-9 data bits (LSB first) → optional parity bit → 1-2 stop bits (logic high). The idle line state is logic high (mark).

column1: What voltage range defines TTL logic levels, and why is this dangerous when interfacing with 3.3V SoCs?
column2: TTL: Logic High ≥2.0V (driven to 5V), Logic Low ≤0.8V (driven to 0V). Connecting a 5V TTL UART directly to a 3.3V SoC GPIO without a level shifter will permanently damage the target.

column1: What is the maximum cumulative timing error allowed across a UART frame per EIA-232/TIA-232, and why?
column2: No more than half a bit period. At 115200 baud (8.68 µs/bit over 10 bits), the allowable cumulative error is ±4.34 µs — exceeding this causes mis-sampling since the receiver loses lock on bit boundaries.

column1: How does a UART receiver determine the correct sampling point within a bit period, and why?
column2: It oversamples the line (typically 16x or 8x baud rate) and samples at the center of the bit period (e.g., sample 8 of 16) using majority voting, maximizing setup/hold margin and rejecting narrow glitches.

column1: Derive the STM32F4 UART BRR register value for 115200 baud with a 42 MHz PCLK in oversampling-by-16 mode.
column2: BRR = 42,000,000 / (16 × 115,200) = 22.786. Mantissa = 22 (0x16), Fraction = round(0.786×16) = 13 (0x0D), giving BRR = 0x016D, actual baud ≈115,107 bps (~0.08% error).

column1: Why does an idle UART TX line sitting at stable high voltage matter during hardware reconnaissance?
column2: Electrical idle (mark) state is logic high; a powered but silent UART TX pin will show a stable high voltage, distinguishing it from an unused/floating GPIO during pin identification.

column1: What three critical capabilities does unauthenticated UART console access typically expose on embedded devices?
column2: 1) Unauthenticated root shell or bootloader prompt before OS authentication, 2) a timed bootloader interrupt window (e.g., U-Boot autoboot countdown) exposing commands like md, mw, sf, nand, bootm, 3) kernel boot logs and crash dumps revealing KASLR offsets, stack addresses, and module lists.

column1: What is the purpose of the WREN (0x06) command in the SPI NOR flash command set?
column2: Write Enable — it must be issued before any program or erase operation on SPI NOR flash; without it, write/erase commands are ignored by the flash's write-protect logic.

column1: What distinguishes RPMB (Replay Protected Memory Block) in eMMC/eUFS storage from standard block storage access?
column2: RPMB provides a cryptographically authenticated, replay-protected memory region requiring a shared key and sequence counter for read/write access, preventing simple replay or extraction via standard block commands.

column1: Why does a baud rate mismatch of only 2-3% cause communication failure over a 10-bit UART frame?
column2: Because there is no shared clock for resynchronization, phase error accumulates bit-by-bit across the frame; a small per-bit timing offset compounds until it exceeds the half-bit-period sampling margin, causing mis-sampled bits.

column1: What is the function of the 0x9F (RDID) command in SPI NOR flash reconnaissance?
column2: Read JEDEC ID — returns the manufacturer ID, memory type, and capacity, allowing an attacker/analyst to identify the exact flash part and its command set/addressing scheme before extraction.
